1.pericope_label: The angel at Bochim, and the covenant charged home
debates: Who the angel of the Lord was: Gill reports the Targum and the Jewish commentators for a prophet, and Phinehas in particular, and rejects it because the speaker claims for himself the bringing of Israel out of Egypt; Henry cites a bishop and a Hebraist for the Angel of the covenant and for Christ; Keil argues from the sacrifice at a place with no sanctuary; and Ellicott, having stated the objection that angels are sent to individuals and prophets to nations, still answers it in favour of the angel
outliers: Henry's observation that Joshua had lately given the same warning and they had disregarded the words of a dying man, so the living God brings it himself, and if they slight his servants surely they will reverence his Son
Ellicott's report that some manuscripts leave a blank at the opening of the speech, as though the formula thus saith the Lord had accidentally fallen out of the text
Ellicott's note that the Hebrew says only they shall be to you for sides, the words as thorns being supplied by conjecture from Numbers
Henry's refusal to be satisfied with the weeping, since they wept and we do not find that they reformed, and many are melted under the word who harden again before they are cast into a new mould

6.pericope_label: Joshua dismisses the people, and a generation arises that knew not the Lord
debates: What the name of the burial place means: Ellicott calls the form used here an accidental transposition of letters for the form in Joshua and holds that the rabbinic story about the sun grew out of the error, while Henry reports the same story and rejects it on the different ground that an image of the sun would have been too dangerous to allow
outliers: Ellicott's report of a tradition preserved in the Greek that the flint knives of the neglected circumcision were buried in Joshua's tomb, and of a later pilgrim's astonishment that the distributor of possessions had chosen rough mountain country for himself

Henry's account of why the good resolutions lasted only one generation, that they held as long as there were rulers to set examples and restrain the corruptions creeping in, and as long as the great works were fresh in memory: those who had seen them believed their own eyes, and those who followed, because they had not seen, believed not

Keil's grammatical point that the verb expresses the order of thought and not of time, so that the repetition from Joshua is placed here to sharpen the contrast between the age that was past and the period now beginning
themes: a generation that knew not the Lord

11.pericope_label: They served Baalim, and the hand of the Lord was against them
debates: What the apostasy actually was: Ellicott judges it a breach rather of the second commandment than of the first, a worship of the Lord under false symbols by a spurious syncretism, and compares the calf-worship of the northern tribes, while Gill, Clarke and Keil read it plainly as forsaking the Lord for other gods

What the phrase about going out means: Gill reports Jewish expositors who take it of military expeditions and the battle going against them, and others who apply it to those who left the land to escape its calamities, naming Elimelech and his sons
outliers: Ellicott's report of the warning in Hosea against the too facile use of the word Baal, where the Lord promises that his people shall call him my husband and no more my lord
Ellicott's caution that the name of the goddess is not to be confused with the word the English renders groves, the two words resembling each other less in Hebrew than in English

Clarke's statement of the aggravation, that they forsook the God who had brought them out of the most grievous oppression by a display of power that should never have been forgotten, and served idols as destitute of real being as of influence
themes: the names of the false gods

16.pericope_label: The Lord raised up judges, and yet they would not hearken
debates: How the repenting of the Lord is to be understood: Clarke reads it as a change of purpose consistent with the terms first announced, the threatened destruction being conditional upon impenitence, while Ellicott reads it as an anthropomorphism which the writers themselves knew to be an imperfect and approximate way of explaining the dealings of God with man

Whether the language of whoredom is figure only: Ellicott takes it simply as the spiritual adultery under which idolatry is everywhere described, while Clarke holds that the impure rites attending many idolatrous practices make the word literally as well as metaphorically proper
outliers: Ellicott's identification of the title of the judges with that of the Phoenician Suffetes, who succeeded the kings and were the doges of Tyre, and his notice that Spanish governors of the middle ages and the chief officer of Sardinia bore the same name

Ellicott's observation that some of the judges, Tola and Ibzan and Elon and Abdon, are credited with no warlike deed at all, and that Samuel, who was no fighter, nevertheless roused the military courage of his people
Clarke's remark that most sinners go through great tribulation in order to get to eternal perdition, and would have had less pain in their way to heaven
Gill's report of the Targum, which renders the clause that the Word of the Lord was for the help of the judge
themes: the Spirit of God upon the judges

20.pericope_label: The anger of the Lord, and the nations left to prove Israel
debates: Why the nations were left: Gill weighs a trial of Israel, to see whether they would give in to the idolatry of the land, against a penal reading in which the nations remain because the covenant had been transgressed, and prefers the first, while the sentence itself and Keil ground the refusal in the covenant breach

Whether the threat was absolute: Keil takes the word hastily to limit it, so that repentance at any point would have recalled the threat and set the extermination going again, while Clarke reads the outcome as simply the withdrawal of a help Israel forfeited by disobedience
outliers: Clarke's apologetic turn at the end, that the failure was never in the promise but in the people, so that the argument of the infidels against revelation drawn from the failure of positive promises and oaths falls to the ground
Ellicott's citation of Ewald, that during the long pause of apparent inaction a hidden movement was going on, and the truths brought to light in the desert were taking firm root
Clarke's figure of a master or a father who, distrusting the fidelity of a servant or a son, places him in circumstances where his conduct will either justify the suspicion or disprove it
Keil's grammatical dispute with Studer and Bertheau over what the purpose clause of the proving of Israel is attached to
